fatal_errors: The initial material is incorrectly treated as a single-phase solid solution rather than the as-cast FCC+B2 AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic alloy.
Mechanical loading is presented as the intervention, omitting the controlling thermal-aging comparison near 600°C and 750°C.
The hypothesis misses the non-monotonic ductile-brittle-ductile transition and the bounded 550-750°C embrittlement window.
The proposed mechanism does not identify enhanced L12 ordering, elevated antiphase-boundary energy, restricted cross-slip, planar slip, or crack initiation at jagged B2/FCC phase-boundary tips.

The cited studies show phase formation in materially different HEAs but do not establish that secondary phases cause the proposed toughness loss; several report strengthening or favorable mechanical properties instead.
The experiment and falsification rule do not isolate precipitate formation from temperature, processing defects, grain-boundary effects, or loading variables.
explanation: The response recognizes the broad possibility that microstructural evolution can alter HEA fracture behavior, but it neither reconstructs the target alloy nor supplies a well-supported alternative mechanism. It gives no specified aging schedule, temperature-resolved control groups, phase-boundary characterization, or prediction of ductility recovery at 750°C. Its measurements are generic and would not distinguish precipitation embrittlement from the target ordering-and-phase-boundary mechanism. A discriminating test would compare as-cast, approximately 600°C-aged, and approximately 750°C-aged specimens under identical tensile conditions, while using TEM or TKD to correlate L12 order, planar dislocation pile-ups, jagged B2/FCC boundary tips, and crack initiation, alongside segregation analysis. The evidence cited supports phase evolution in other HEAs but not the claimed causal link to brittle fracture.
